name: Chipaya
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Cerrón-Palomino, Rodolfo. 2006. El chipaya o la lengua de los hombres del agua. Lima: Fondo Editorial, Pontificia Universidad Católica del Perú. xviii+309 pp. ISBN 9972-42-771-4. Open-access publisher PDF, PUCP repository, DOI 10.18800/9972427714. (Second-hand corroboration: García Chinchay, Francisco. 2012. Review of Cerrón-Palomino 2006. LIAMES 7(1): 103-108, p. 104.)
catalog_locator: Cap. II Fonología, § 4 'El acento de intensidad', pp. 66-69 (pp. 84-87 of the copy consulted); rule p. 66 last paragraph, examples and apocope cases pp. 67-68, infinitives p. 69
catalog_quote: 4. El acento de intensidad. Como ocurre en las lenguas andinas mayores, en el chipaya también el rasgo culminativo o acento de intensidad se localiza de manera fija en la penúltima sílaba de la palabra, y, por consiguiente, no tiene valor distintivo. De esta manera, pues, normalmente, las palabras de la lengua son llanas o graves, por lo que no hace falta emplear tildes de ninguna clase al momento de proceder con su escritura. Los ejemplos que siguen son elementos léxicos irreductibles con la acentuación penúltima esperada: añi [áñi] ‘temporada lluviosa’ kerka [kérka] ‘armadillo’ akuλa [akúλa] ‘sapo joven’ ketwana [ketwána] ‘conejo silvestre’ tsukunta [tsukúnta] ‘susto’ ... [p. 67] todo elemento modificador que precede a su núcleo pierde su vocal final, siempre y cuando ésta no vaya precedida de más de una consonante. Como resultado de ello, el modificador, fonéticamente trunco, acaba portando una acentuación aguda ... En tales casos, efectivamente, el acento de intensidad no se retrae, ya que permanece en su posición original, a despecho de la reestructuración silábica automática del elemento modificador. ... [p. 68] esta vez el acento, una vez producido el apócope de la vocal de los sufijos, se retrae automáticamente a la posición penúltima, de acuerdo con la regla general establecida.

new_statements.translation: 4. Intensity stress. As in the major Andean languages, in Chipaya too the culminative feature or intensity stress is located in a fixed way on the penultimate syllable of the word, and consequently has no distinctive value. Thus, normally, the words of the language are paroxytone, so there is no need to use written accent marks of any kind when writing it. [p. 67:] ... every modifier that precedes its head loses its final vowel ... As a result, the phonetically truncated modifier ends up bearing final (oxytone) stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary (intensity) stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the word and is non-contrastive; words are canonically paroxytone (examples p. 67: [áñi], [kérka], [akúλa], [ketwána], [tsukúnta]). Surface oxytones arise only from vowel apocope: prenominal modifiers and pre-pausal suffixed forms lose their final vowel but keep stress on the underlying penult ([paták wáλpa] 'cien gallinas', [taxa-úk] 'hacia el oeste'), and infinitives in -ş are oxytone for the same historical reason; when the vowel is restored (e.g. by adding -mi) stress reappears on the underlying penult. In apocopated case-suffixed forms, by contrast, stress retracts to the surface penult ([óñ-ki] 'al hombre', [pampí-kin]).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the section (no reference to secondary stress anywhere in the grammar).
new_statements.exceptions: Apocope-induced final stress in prenominal modifiers, pre-pausal truncated forms and -ş infinitives (stress stays on underlying penult); apocopated case-marked forms retract to the surface penult (author's analysis: those case suffixes are reinterpreted as consonant-final).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('la penúltima sílaba de la palabra'); examples are isolated lexical items plus phrasal modifier+head sequences and suffixed forms before pause; the author compares the pattern to Quechua and Aymara.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes the Chipaya of Santa Ana de Chipaya (Oruro, Bolivia), the only living Uru-Chipaya language, based on the author's own fieldwork (principal consultants Máximo Felipe Lázaro and Filemón Felipe Mamani); this matches chip1262 directly. Not to be confused with Uchumataqu/Uru of Irohito (uruu1244), the extinct sister language.

sources.note: Cap. II Fonología § 4 'El acento de intensidad', pp. 66-69: intensity stress falls fixedly on the penultimate syllable of the word and is not distinctive; words are normally paroxytone; apocope of final vowels (prenominal modifiers, pre-pausal truncation, infinitive -ş) yields surface oxytones because stress stays on the underlying penult, whereas apocopated case-suffixed forms retract stress to the surface penult.
